craft_claim: Stylistic deviation and parallelism (foregrounding) produce measurable affective response and slow reading into an aesthetic mode of attention, which is how lyrical passages become salient.

supporting_evidence.note: Miall and Kuiken found that foregrounding (deviation and parallelism) predicts affective response to literary stories and is associated with slower reading and aesthetic attention.

counterevidence.note: Effortful disfluency can lower liking, so foregrounding beyond a threshold is self-defeating; the affective effect is not monotonic.

scope: Literary prose and verse; local passages, since sustained foregrounding is not tolerable across long spans.
exceptions: Readers under speed pressure, who experience foregrounding as obstruction rather than affect.
